variants.name: ECMAScript # private fields with getters
variants.implementation_notes: A `#`-prefixed class field is enforced by the JavaScript engine: it cannot be referenced outside the class body, is not inherited by subclasses (a subclass declaring `#data` creates an unrelated field), and is invisible to `Object.keys`, `JSON.stringify`, property lookup and `structuredClone`. Pair it with a getter and the object is readable but not writable from anywhere outside - the pattern's strongest available form in JavaScript. `Object.freeze` complements it when the holder must also resist writes from the class's own methods: freezing makes the object's own data properties non-writable and non-configurable, but it is shallow, so nested objects must be frozen recursively or replaced by immutable values.
pitfalls: `Object.freeze` is shallow and does not affect private fields: a frozen holder can still contain a mutable array, and the class's own methods can still reassign `#data`.
Private names are scoped to the class body, so subclasses - and any code that receives the instance - cannot read the state; extension has to go through the base class's accessors.
`#` fields are not own properties: `JSON.stringify`, `structuredClone`, spread and many mapping libraries silently ignore them, so serialization needs explicit methods.

variants.name: Closure- or WeakMap-backed private data (pre-ES2022)
variants.idiom_name: module-scoped WeakMap keyed by the instance
variants.implementation_notes: Before private fields, the state was kept in a module- or closure-scoped `WeakMap` keyed by the instance (or captured by an IIFE), and only methods closed over that map could reach it; subclasses and serializers see nothing, which gives the same read/write asymmetry at the price of one WeakMap lookup per access and no own properties on the instance. This is still the shape emitted when `#` fields are downlevelled below ES2015, so it remains the compatibility form rather than a historical curiosity. Prefer `#` fields where the target supports them; keep the WeakMap form for older runtimes or when state must be shared between classes that cannot see each other's private names.
pitfalls: WeakMap-backed state is invisible to `JSON.stringify`, `structuredClone` and property enumeration, and the key must stay reachable or the entry is collected - serialization needs explicit methods.
Any function with the map in scope can write the entry, so the guarantee is module hygiene rather than enforcement, and a missed `data.get` on a detached object throws at runtime.
Downlevelled `#` fields compile to this exact pattern, so mixing both styles in one hierarchy makes debugging the same state twice unnecessarily confusing.
